title: Who am I (Exodus 3:11–4:17)
hookLine: Moses gives five excuses, including I'm slow of speech

cards: Moses is standing barefoot before a burning bush, and God has just told him the plan: I've seen my people's misery in Egypt, I've heard their cry, and I'm sending you to Pharaoh to bring them out.

Some jobs arrive too big for the person asked, and the reasons it should be someone else line up fast, every one of them reasonable. And Moses, who will lead a whole people out of slavery, does what people do.
He makes excuses. Five of them.

teach.h: WHO AM I? I WILL BE WITH THEE.
teach.b: Excuse one: who am I, to go to Pharaoh? A fair question from a shepherd with a past. God doesn't answer it.
God doesn't say, you're actually very talented. God says, "I will be with thee." The answer to who am I is who goes with you.
Excuse two: what if they ask your name? God gives the name, I am who am, which this path opened back in year one.
Excuse three: they won't believe me. So God gives signs: the staff that becomes a snake, the hand that turns white and heals, Nile water that turns to blood.

teach.h: I'M SLOW OF SPEECH: WHO MADE YOUR MOUTH?
teach.b: Excuse four is the most human: I'm not a speaker, not before and not since you started talking to me; I'm slow of speech and slow of tongue.
Some Jewish tradition and some later readers have wondered whether Moses had a stammer; the text doesn't say. God's reply is almost funny: who made a person's mouth? Go, and I'll be with your mouth.

teach.h: SEND SOMEONE ELSE: AARON GOES TOO.
teach.b: Then excuse five, with nothing left: please, Lord, send someone else. That one makes God angry. And still God doesn't fire him.
God sends his brother Aaron along to help him speak. Catholics hear an echo of this scene in a small house in Nazareth.

An angel greets a young woman with the words, "the Lord is with thee," and gives her an impossible mission. She asks one honest question, how shall this be done, gets her answer, and says yes. Moses took five tries.
The promise was the same both times: you won't go alone.

how: Catholics pray the angel's greeting to Mary, "the Lord is with thee," in every Hail Mary, and the Church often reads call stories like Moses's on vocation Sundays, when parishes pray for priests, religious and lay ministers.

o: Moses's brother, sent along to help him speak
Moses's father-in-law, a priest of Midian
the shepherd who taught Moses the signs

games.q: match each excuse to God's answer.
p: the staff, the hand, the water

s: God answers who am I by telling Moses how gifted he is
God answers with presence: I will be with thee.
the text says plainly that Moses had a stammer
he says he's slow of speech and tongue. whether it was a stammer, the text doesn't say.
Moses's last excuse made God angry, but God still sent him
send someone else, he says. God is angry, and sends Aaron with him.

games.q: you're Moses. you've run out of reasons. God has answered every one. what's your last line?
o: let me think about it for a year.
games.why: he asks God to send someone else. God is angry, and sends him anyway, with his brother Aaron to help him speak.

practice: Think of one thing you've been avoiding because it feels too big, a call, an apology, a class, a conversation, and say your reason plainly, the way Moses did: I'm not good with words, I'm not the right person, they won't listen.

Don't argue with it; picture yourself doing the thing anyway, excuse and all, with someone beside you. If you pray, hear God's answer to Moses, I will be with thee; if you don't, picture a friend at your shoulder.

wordCard.voice: Aaron. The brother God sends along to help Moses speak, after five excuses at the burning bush and one promise of presence. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: who am I? Moses's first words of reply in Exodus 3:11.

carryVoice: Your line: I will be with thee. Five excuses, and one promise under all of them. Day three hundred seventy, done.
